Who Needs Whom? Apple and the Chinese State

Stephen Weymouth

Dean’s Professor

2026-10-14

In May 2016 Beijing summoned Tim Cook to Zhongnanhai. He brought a $275 billion pledge.

Timing: 0–3 minutes. Zhongnanhai is the Communist Party’s headquarters in central Beijing. Cook came with Jeff Williams, Apple’s operations chief, and Lisa Jackson, head of Environment, Policy, and Social Initiatives. The meeting was with the National Development and Reform Commission; the pledge covered five years. Cook had been there before, in March 2012, to meet Li Keqiang. Wednesday, September 30, ended with Isabel Ge Mahe as Apple’s “face of China”; Module 5 asks what firms and governments want from each other.

[Sources] - Patrick McGee, Apple in China (2025), ch. 31, pp. 278, 280. Background photograph: Jorge Láscar, Xinhua Gate (Xinhuamen), November 25, 2008, Flickr via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Lascar_Xinhua_Gate_(Xinhuamen)_(4497575335).jpg, resized. The banners at either side of the gate are the two McGee describes.

Your IB Voice

Weigh the leverage

Apple’s suppliers employed more than a million Chinese workers, yet Beijing could hurt Apple almost whenever it chose. In 2016, who needed whom more: Apple or the Chinese state?

10 minutes · Individual · Notes permitted

Timing: 3–13 minutes. Leave the prompt up for the full ten minutes. The passages students will reach for: the labor dispatch law (pp. 260–262), the CSR score and the tax claim (pp. 263–264), the pledge (pp. 280–283), and the Tesla factory (pp. 286–288). Do not preview the hypotheses.

[Sources] - McGee (2025), chs. 27, 29, 31, pp. 244–250, 259–266, 278–288.

Competing explanations

Who needed whom more in 2016?

Apple needed China more, because its whole supply chain was there.

China needed Apple more, because Apple’s suppliers employed and trained millions.

Beijing held the leverage, because it wrote the rules and chose when to enforce them.

Apple held the leverage, because it could move production to another country.

What evidence in the chapters would tell these claims apart?

Timing: 13–16 minutes. Take three or four responses before revealing the list, and write each claim on the board in the room’s words. Keep the board for the takeaways. Press on the last claim: the chapters give no sign that Apple threatened to leave.

[Sources] - McGee (2025), chs. 27, 29, 31.

What could Beijing do to Apple?

Timing: 16–16 minutes.

Doug Guthrie saw that China wanted something

INMA/Jarle Naustvik, Doug Guthrie, Building the Creative Organization, Gulltaggen 2010, 2010 · Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

Until 2013 suppliers such as Foxconn dealt with provincial officials, and no Apple executive lived in China.

Guthrie, a Mandarin-speaking scholar of China’s local institutions, joined Apple in 2013 and asked to be sent to Shanghai.

He read Beijing’s pressure as a demand Apple had not met.

Timing: 16–19 minutes. Guthrie became dean of George Washington University’s business school in 2010, aged thirty-nine, and was fired in 2013 over a budget dispute; Joel Podolny of Apple University recruited him. On the CCTV attack of 2013: “China wanted something from Apple, he surmised, and Cook’s apology hadn’t delivered.” His condition: “But send me to Shanghai.” The Gang of Eight (three new hires and five Apple executives) included Rory Sexton, the first Apple vice president to live in China, Steve Marcher, and Jun Ge, who knew Pudong’s administration was separate from Shanghai’s. When the Times reported the Zhengzhou incentives, Apple said “it was not a party” to the negotiations, and it was true. The photograph is identified by its Commons title; it shows Guthrie in 2010, three years before he joined Apple.

[Sources] - McGee (2025), ch. 27, pp. 244–250. Photo: INMA/Jarle Naustvik, Gulltaggen conference, April 28, 2010, Flickr via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0, resized.

“You’re supposed to be out of compliance.”

Timing: 19–21 minutes. Guthrie to Apple’s lawyers about the labor dispatch law of mid-2014, enforceable from March 2016, which capped temporary workers at 10 percent of a company’s workforce. The rest of the exchange: “How does that make any sense?” “Because you’re supposed to go figure out what the mayor of Zhengzhou wants from you.” Ask the room what the mayor might want before moving on. The photograph is the gate of the Zhengzhou Airport Economy Zone, where Foxconn’s “iPhone City” sits, in 2018.

[Sources] - McGee (2025), ch. 29, pp. 260–261. Background photograph: Windmemories, The sign of Zhengzhou Airport Economy Zone at Yingbin Elevated Road, June 14, 2018, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:ZAEZ_gate.jpg, resized.

A labor law Apple’s suppliers could not obey

Nearly half of 362 supplier factories broke the 10 percent cap, and 80 used temporary workers for over half their staff.

The law was national but enforced locally, so each city chose which factory to punish.

McGee, Apple in China (2025), p. 261, citing internal Apple documents; third bar is the instructor’s arithmetic.

A rule that almost everyone breaks lets the state press one factory at a time.

Timing: 21–24 minutes. Chart: Apple’s need for Chinese labor fell “below 900,000 in the slow months of spring” and rose to “more than 1.7 million in the peak season before iPhone launch.” The third bar assumes the off-peak workforce is permanent: 900,000 / 0.9 is about 1.0 million, so the true allowed peak is lower still. During ramp some factories’ temporary share exceeded 80 percent. The 2015 Apple presentation: “10% dispatch is simply not enough to cope with the spikes in labor demand we require during our ramps.” McGee: Apple’s three choices were to overhaul its business, leave China, or “find out what the local officials wanted”; “voluntary is the new mandatory.” The “floating population” was more than 220 million adult workers.

[Sources] - McGee (2025), ch. 29, pp. 261–263. Chart: series in instructor/2026-10-14-series.json; original drawing.

Apple scored lowest of all large multinationals

22.5

out of 100 was Apple’s score in the state’s first corporate responsibility ranking, in 2015

Apple was the only foreign firm on the list not labeled a joint venture. Samsung, with Chinese partners, scored best.

The score measured what Apple shared with Chinese firms, not its environmental record.

Timing: 24–27 minutes. The ranking was published by SASAC, the State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission, the largest shareholder of China Mobile and China Telecom. About forty companies were ranked. Cupertino’s lawyers asked Guthrie why, citing Apple’s work on toxic chemicals and carbon; his answer was that they were missing the point. The same year: engineers fined on the spot over visa rules, supplies stopped between factories (“bu fang bian,” inconvenience), and in September 2015 a Ministry of Finance claim of more than $80 million in unpaid taxes and fines. Guthrie’s summary: “We’re watching you. And just like on Consumer Day, we can hit you if we want.”

[Sources] - McGee (2025), ch. 29, pp. 263–264.

Signals

Beijing sent a tax bill, a low score, a labor law, and fines on Apple’s engineers. Was any one of these a serious threat?

If none was, why did Cupertino read them together as a warning?

Timing: 27–31 minutes. Expected answers to the first question: no single one was; $80 million was small against a $216 billion cash pile, and the labor law was never enforced with fines. Expected answers to the second: together they showed that the state could hurt Apple in many places at once, that it chose when to act, and that it wanted something Apple had not offered; the precedent of Microsoft, Qualcomm, IBM, and Cisco, each of which ended up with a joint venture or a technology transfer, made the signal readable. Hold the answers for the Qualcomm slide.

[Sources] - McGee (2025), ch. 29, pp. 264–266; ch. 31, p. 279.

Qualcomm could not walk away from China

Qualcomm earns a fee on every smartphone using its technology, and over half its revenue came from China.

In 2015 it paid a $975 million fine and agreed to a joint venture.

QUALCOMM Inc. and Apple Inc., Forms 10-K, fiscal 2015, revenue by customer location and by segment.

In a firm-government bargain, each side’s leverage is what it could withhold that the other could not replace.

Timing: 31–34 minutes. Chart: Qualcomm’s revenue from customers based in China (including Hong Kong) was 53 percent in fiscal 2015 ($13.3 billion of $25.3 billion), 49 percent in 2013, 57 in 2016, and 65 in 2017; Apple’s Greater China share was 25 percent ($58.7 billion of $233.7 billion). Qualcomm’s figure counts where the customer is based, including handset makers that export, and Apple’s includes Taiwan. The $975 million fine was the largest in China’s corporate history. A Qualcomm executive: “They held us hostage for a billion dollars and stole our intellectual property. And there was no negotiating. We were just grateful that we got to keep our business model.” For ten days Qualcomm stopped sending people to China; its one negotiator slept on the company jet. The definition on the key-line is the instructor’s.

[Sources] - McGee (2025), ch. 29, pp. 265–266. QUALCOMM Incorporated, Form 10-K for fiscal 2015 (filed November 4, 2015) and fiscal 2017, revenues by country; Apple Inc., Form 10-K for fiscal 2015, net sales by reportable segment; retrieved from sec.gov September 29, 2026; original drawing.

What did Apple have that Beijing wanted?

Timing: 34–34 minutes.

Apple went to Beijing needing China badly

Apple Inc., Forms 10-Q and 10-K, fiscal 2015 to 2017, net sales by reportable segment.

Sales fell for six straight quarters from early 2016, and in April regulators shut Apple’s new iTunes and iBooks stores.

The weaker Apple’s position in the market, the more it needed something the state valued.

Timing: 34–37 minutes. Chart, billions of dollars by quarter ending: December 2014 16.1, March 2015 16.8, June 13.2, September 12.5, December 2015 18.4, March 2016 12.5, June 8.8, September 8.8, December 2016 16.2, March 2017 10.7, June 8.0, September 9.8. The March 2016 quarter was down 26 percent on a year earlier and pushed Apple to its first decline in global revenue in thirteen years; shares fell 7.9 percent. Six quarters of decline followed, and iPhone’s share of China’s market fell from 15 to 9 percent. In the holiday quarter of 2015 China sales had grown 14 percent while global revenue grew 2 percent. The regulator said Apple would need a joint-venture partner to run the services. Fourth quarters are the 10-K annual figure less the first three quarters.

[Sources] - McGee (2025), ch. 31, pp. 279–280. Apple Inc., Forms 10-Q for fiscal 2015 Q1 to fiscal 2017 Q3 and Forms 10-K for fiscal 2015 to 2017, Greater China net sales; retrieved from sec.gov September 29, 2026; original drawing.

Apple’s pledge was twice the Marshall Plan

McGee, Apple in China (2025), p. 281; comparisons in 2016 dollars as McGee gives them.

The $275 billion was Apple’s estimate of $55 billion spent in China in 2015, multiplied by five years, so it promised nothing new.

What changed in 2016 was not Apple’s investment but what Beijing was told about it.

Timing: 37–40 minutes. Chart: Apple’s pledge $275 billion over five years; the Marshall Plan $13.3 billion over four years for sixteen countries, “or $131 billion in 2016 dollars”; Japan’s Overseas Economic Cooperation Fund loans to China, 1979 to 2007, ¥2.54 trillion, “around $30 billion in 2016 dollars.” McGee also says the pledge exceeded all Canadian and U.S. private investment in Mexico from NAFTA’s signing through 2020. The pledge was a nonbinding memorandum of understanding of 1,250 words, drafted by David McIntosh in Cupertino from work by Guthrie, Marcher, and Jun Ge. Cook delivered it quietly: Trump was campaigning on 45 percent tariffs and “Apple to build their damn computers” in the United States. McGee: “the five-year pledge would rightly be seen as a low-ball projection, given that it assumed no growth.”

[Sources] - McGee (2025), ch. 31, pp. 280–284. Chart: series in instructor/2026-10-14-series.json; original drawing.

Apple’s real offer was know-how, not money

4,000

engineers worked in Apple’s China operations team within a few years of 2013, up from 1,000

Apple trained suppliers, brought them machines from Europe and Japan, and bought all they made.

No government program could do that, and the skills stayed with the suppliers.

Timing: 40–43 minutes. McGee: “In economic terms, Apple was creating the whole market,” supplying training and machinery and then “purchasing the outputs.” Engineers came from MIT, Caltech, and Stanford or from Tesla, Dell, and Motorola, and worked up to eighteen hours a day. The Subject Matter Experts team searched watch and jewelry industries in Switzerland, Germany, and Austria for machines to adapt. Apple’s advanced-electronics investment was “by far the most important” thing Xi wanted, according to Barry Naughton. The memo’s message was “music to the ears of China,” and McGee calls Apple “the biggest corporate supporter of Made in China 2025.” Tacit knowledge in Yi Wen’s words: know-how “in the art of making things.”

[Sources] - McGee (2025), ch. 27, pp. 245–246; ch. 31, pp. 281–285.

Secrecy

If Apple’s know-how was so valuable to China, why did Apple have to tell Beijing about it?

What does the answer suggest about secrecy as a bargaining strategy?

Timing: 43–47 minutes. Expected answers to the first question: Apple had been secretive (few knew its suppliers before it published a list in 2012), the transfer was largely unintentional, and it ran through suppliers such as Foxconn rather than through a joint venture that officials could see. Expected answers to the second: leverage counts only if the other side knows what it would lose; secrecy protected Apple from rivals and from U.S. politics but cost it standing in Beijing, which is why Cook told the state quietly rather than holding a press conference. Tie back to the CSR slide: the missing “joint venture” label was the visible sign of what Beijing thought it was not getting.

[Sources] - McGee (2025), ch. 29, p. 264; ch. 31, pp. 280, 283.

China’s exports once relied on foreign firms

Ministry of Commerce of the People’s Republic of China, Statistical Bulletin of FDI in China 2023, Appendix 13.

From 2001 to 2011 foreign-invested firms made more than half of what China sold abroad, so Beijing’s growth depended on them.

Two sides are mutually dependent when each would lose from a break, and the side that would lose less holds more leverage.

Timing: 47–50 minutes. Chart: exports by foreign-invested enterprises as a share of China’s total, 12.6 percent in 1990, 47.9 in 2000, 58.3 in 2005 (the peak), 54.6 in 2010, 44.2 in 2015, 36.0 in 2020, 31.5 in 2022. Foxconn, Pegatron, and Apple’s other Taiwanese assemblers count as foreign-invested. Ask: which way was the line moving when Cook went to Zhongnanhai in 2016, and what does that say about who was gaining leverage? The definition on the key-line is the instructor’s. Retrieved September 29, 2026.

[Sources] - Ministry of Commerce of the People’s Republic of China, Statistical Bulletin of FDI in China 2023, Appendix 13, Imports and Exports by FIEs, 1986–2022; original drawing.

Once China has learned, who needs whom?

Timing: 50–50 minutes.

In 2018 Shanghai let Tesla build a car plant with no Chinese partner, a first for a foreign carmaker.

Timing: 50–52 minutes. The press called it a sweetheart deal; McGee says China “was acting in its own interest.” The mayor of Shanghai talked Musk from two years down to twelve months, with cheap land and tax benefits. Ground broke in December 2018 and China-made Model 3s left the line by late 2019; the Model 3 was China’s best-selling EV in 2020, and Shanghai now makes half of Tesla’s cars. The photograph is the Shanghai assembly line in 2023.

[Sources] - McGee (2025), ch. 31, pp. 286–288. Background photograph: China News Service, Tesla Gigafactory Shanghai assembly line, May 30, 2023, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tesla_Gigafactory_Shanghai_assembly_line_01.png, resized.

Joint ventures did not teach China to build cars

ChengH, 1983 Shanghai-Volkswagen Santana, 2015 · Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

From 1984 foreign carmakers entered China through joint ventures meant to teach Chinese partners to build and export.

By 2016 Germans held over 70 percent of the premium market, and no Chinese brand competed abroad.

A share of the profits did not give Chinese partners the know-how.

Timing: 52–55 minutes. The Guangming Daily in 1985: replace “the first machine imported, the second machine imported, and third machine imported” with “the first machine imported, the second made in China, and third machine exported.” In 2016 all ten premium brand leaders in China were foreign. The Economist: “For all its manufacturing might, China never mastered internal-combustion engines.” McGee: Apple’s model “left Chinese officials convinced that its JV model was broken.” The key-line is the instructor’s reading. The car is the first Shanghai Volkswagen model, in a museum.

[Sources] - McGee (2025), ch. 31, p. 286. Photo: ChengH, July 19, 2015, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0, resized.

Tesla’s suppliers learned to build for BYD

Tesla trained local suppliers that also serve Chinese carmakers such as BYD, which McGee calls the Apple model.

Half of China’s new cars are now electric, twice Europe’s share.

International Energy Agency, Global EV Data Explorer, EV sales share of new cars.

Leverage shifts toward the state as local firms learn what the foreign firm once brought.

Timing: 55–58 minutes. Chart, electric share of new car sales, percent: China 5 in 2019, 16 in 2021, 29 in 2022, 38 in 2023, 48 in 2024, 53 in 2025; Europe 3.4 in 2019 and 28 in 2025; United States 2.1 in 2019 and 10 in 2025. McGee gives 4.8 percent in 2019 and 38 percent in 2023 for EVs and plug-ins. The “catfish effect”: one predator in the tank keeps the sardines swimming; McGee calls the theory “partly misleading,” because Tesla improves the vendors who then supply BYD. A former Tesla executive says one U.S. company wins in each industry, Tesla in cars and Apple in phones, while “all the Chinese companies win.” The definition on the key-line is the instructor’s; it sets up next Monday. Retrieved September 29, 2026.

[Sources] - McGee (2025), ch. 31, pp. 287–288. International Energy Agency, Global EV Data Explorer (api.iea.org/evs), EV sales share, cars, historical, China, Europe, USA; original drawing.

Who needs whom in your industry?

Timing: 58–58 minutes. Teams sit together. Each team works from the system diagram it submitted on October 5, which shows which activities firms own, buy, or run with partners.

Decide who needs whom in your industry

  1. Select one firm in your team’s network and one government whose decisions it depends on.
  2. Diagnose what each side could withhold from the other, and which of those the other could replace.
  3. Recommend one thing the firm could show that government about its contribution, in terms the government values.
  4. Defend your answer to who needs whom more, and name what would change it.

15 minutes · Industry teams · Diagrams permitted

Timing: 58–73 minutes. Circulate. For a service firm the government’s levers are licenses, data rules, and visas rather than labor law; the firm’s are jobs, tax, know-how, and access to foreign markets. Push teams that name only what the firm wants from the government to name what the government wants from the firm. Warn at ten minutes. Each team reports the firm, the government, and the one thing that would shift the balance.

[Sources] - Industry Project Briefing (materials/industry-project-briefing.tex); McGee (2025), chs. 29 and 31.

Report out

Where did your team find that the government needs the firm more than the firm needs it?

What would make that leverage run out?

Timing: 73–79 minutes. Take three teams. Expected answers to the key-line: local firms learn the skill, the state finds a second supplier, the firm’s product becomes a commodity, or the firm’s investment becomes impossible to move. Write the last answer on the board; next Monday starts from it.

[Sources] - Team work.

Takeaways

Who needed whom?

Apple needed China’s flexible workforce, and Beijing could threaten it with rules it chose when to enforce.

China needed Apple’s know-how, but Beijing valued it only once Apple described it in Beijing’s terms.

The $275 billion pledge promised no new money, but it told Beijing what it was already getting.

As Chinese firms learn, China needs any one foreign firm less.

Next Monday asks who holds the leverage once a firm’s money is in the ground.

Timing: 79–90 minutes. Before revealing the lines, return to the board from the start of class and cold-call three or four students on their opening responses: which of the room’s claims survived the chapters? Expected: the first two survived in part, the third is closest to McGee’s account, and the fourth has no support in these chapters. Close in open discussion on whether Apple could still threaten to leave China today. Next Monday’s reading is Cohen, The Fish That Ate the Whale, chs. 8 to 12.

[Sources] - McGee (2025), chs. 27, 29, 31.
